speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to ask Your Honour's leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order No. 26 in order to discuss a matter of very urgent national importance, namely the right of this government, through the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, to say in writing to the provinces of Canada that the government will not be able to honour a cost sharing agreement for the building of vocational training schools throughout Canada which it made with the provinces last August. I realize, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I realize it is my task to convince you that it is urgent that we postpone the business of the house to debate this matter; that is, it must be of national importance and must be urgent.
First of all I should like to point out how important it is from a national point of view. Every province in Canada is affected; every person of school age is affected. This concerns the financial structure not only of every province in Canada but also of this government. I do not think there is any doubt concerning the national scope of this subject; therefore I shall leave that matter at this point.
With regard to the matter of urgency I should like to draw to Your Honour's attention the fact that nothing can be more urgent than a question concerning Canada's credit rating. Second, what could be more urgent than a discussion of a matter which concerns the integrity of an individual or a nation

February 13, 1968
Vocational Training
when that integrity is brought into question because of the very fact that the government has told these provinces it cannot fulfil its commitments and cannot honour the agreements. Third, no indication has been given to this house as to when we might have an opportunity to debate this very point. I realize that the estimates were tabled yesterday, but we have not been told when we might expect to have a debate on those estimates or when a supply motion will be called. Therefore we have not been given assurance that this will be done immediately. This very serious problem should be discussed now.
Another reason for the urgency relates particularly to the province of Ontario. The Ontario legislature opens tomorrow. The provincial government must be prepared to budget its expenditures for the year.
That province was promised some $71 million and now is told it will have to find $34 million, which means that this province will have to make some very fast decisions in order to raise this money. Therefore the matter is very urgent. Indeed it is urgent in respect of all provinces and not just Ontario.	>
This- problem is doubly urgent because it affects all provinces. I realize, as I am sure most members of this house realize, the great domino effect this action will have on all provinces across Canada. Therefore it is most urgent that this action be stopped immediately and that we have an opportunity to debate this financial question which has appeared on the horizon.
The sixth reason I believe it is urgent is that we as members of this house have a right to know now just how serious this whole matter is. We have a right to know whether we are just seeing the top of the iceberg. I believe we are entitled to have a full fledged debate on this matter now.
My final point in stressing that it is urgent is that the unemployment situation in Canada is such that every step must be taken to provide training for the unemployed by means of the vocational training schools. Therefore it is most important that this matter be settled speedily so the Minister of Manpower and Immigration will have an opportunity to reconsider the letter he sent to the provinces stating his inability to pay the amounts agreed upon.
With these remarks I hope I have proven to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter of national importance and one of urgency. If you should grant the motion so there would be a postponement of the business for today I

and many other members of this house would welcome the opportunity to speak on this very serious matter.

speechtext:
should like on behalf of the members of this party, Mr. Speaker, to support the motion and urge Your Honour to allow it on the grounds of urgent public importance. In the first place the provinces, who are now in the process of preparing their estimates and their budgets, ought to know exactly what the position is and why this government finds it necessary to curtail the financial commitments it made to the provinces of this country. At the present time in most of the communities I have visited there is a long list of students waiting to get into vocational training schools. The provinces are anxious to meet this problem. They cannot meet it unless they know what the situation is with regard to the financial commitments the federal government is going to keep.
I want to point out also that the matter is important because in this technological age vocational training is becoming increasingly important. If we are to avoid inflation it can only be done by increased productivity, and productivity depends upon training technical staff and workers so they can perform technical functions in industry. This is a matter of great importance all across the country.
I submit to Your Honour that there will be no other opportunity in the immediate future, within the next day or two, to discuss this matter. If we leave it for several days that will be too late. I think the house and the country, particularly the provincial governments, are entitled to a full statement from the government. They are entitled to have that statement made today. We are entitled to know why the government, under the guise of controlling inflation, is seeking to do the very thing that will make inflation worse than it is now. We therefore support this motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my view the House of Commons was treated last evening to a most unusual and remarkable performance by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall). Indeed, after close examination of the text of his speech I have come to the conclusion that he was either poorly informed on the matter before the house or undertook a course of action which in my view can only be called courageous. He advocated a course of action for parliament and the government that flies in the face of 100 years of traditional sentiment and agitation from the area he represents. Surely it takes a courageous man to dissociate himself publicly from the viewpoints and philosophy

of government that have been deeply embedded in the region he represents. The matter before the house, the changing of the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act, represents in a sense an expression of a particular philosophy of government.
It may be said that the situation in the drug industry is such that the framework of the industry needs to be altered. One of the major changes under this measure would lead to freer trade. The hon. member for Halifax, contrary to what may be the understandable wishes of his constituents, has attacked this legislation. He has used arguments which have been primarily used by the drug industry located in central Canada. Thus for the first time we have seen-and I think this is a good balance-a member from the Atlantic region defending the interests of another region at the expense of his own. The approach of the hon. member for Halifax was also in direct contradiction to the stands taken in this house by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) who have attempted to model themselves as particular spokesmen for the interests of their region.

speechtext: Why don't you crawl out from under that rug and stand up?

Let us, therefore, examine some of the arguments which have been brought forth. First of all, the hon. member places great reliance upon the safety issue. Of course, safety is like


motherhood. As I said last evening, it is good debating technique, if you are on otherwise weak ground, to attempt to find an emotional argument that will obscure and cloud the facts. This is an understandable tactic which from time to time a great many people in all walks of life find it necessary to adopt. But in actual fact the overwhelming body of evidence in a series of inquiries suggests the quite obvious fact that in patent legislation safety and quality are two different things. Patent legislation in effect gives a monopoly. It is a sort of economic device which gives a monopoly that has had an inflating effect on the cost of drugs. Safety and quality are covered by the Food and Drugs Act.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It seems to me that if there are problems with regard to safety, quality and control they must relate to the food and drug directorate. In fact, one of the ingredients of the package proposed by the government is an increase in the facilities of the food and drug directorate so that it will be able to deal with the present and future situation. So the hon. member for Halifax, together with the drug industry, has brought the red herring of safety into this debate.
The second argument used by the industry, and again used by the hon. member for Halifax in his defence of the industry, is that research and development naturally lead to higher costs and therefore since it is necessary to conduct research in a research oriented industry this in the end affects the price to the consumer, and in effect the steps the government is proposing to take through this legislation would wipe out research in Canada. It is further argued that it is socially desirable that Canada encourage research. I think everybody agrees with that. It is like motherhood, and we all agree with that. It is said further that the lack of patent protection will lead to secrecy and less courageous investment. These are allegations made by the drug industry and by the junior member for Halifax.
It is understandable that the drug industry would perhaps balk at any changes in the present framework. Under the present system their average profit in the last 12 years has been approximately double that of other manufacturing industries. In taking his courageous stand the hon. member for Halifax has asked his constituents in Halifax to live with this situation. It is understandable that the drug industry would not welcome changes

that would affect the balance. This is understandable from their point of view. But it seems to me it is the responsibility of parliament and the government in this matter to lay the framework and ground rules to make this industry more productive.
In their reports the Hall commission and other commissions have pointed out that in fact very little research is actually carried on in Canada. In the evidence before the standing committee which studied this matter and in the evidence given before other bodies it was pointed out that there are other factors which determine the location where research is carried on. The drug industry is a world wide industry. The drug manufacturers are not interested particularly in the markets of one or another country; they are world wide. Therefore there are other economic factors which dictate the location of their major research facilities. In fact, the evidence given before the committee quite clearly pointed out that it is a fallacious argument to link the patent laws with research. This is the second red herring introduced quite understandably by the drug industry but not quite so understandably by the junior member for Halifax who seems to be so afraid of any change that he will support any existing system on the basis that the devil you know is better than the devil you don't know, while in the meantime his constituents in Nova Scotia and all our constituents must pay among the highest prices in the world for drugs.
The evidence which has been collected by means of the various studies shows that approximately 7 per cent of the manufacturers' dollar is spent on research. This is not a very high figure, particularly when one relates it to the fact that they spend 30 per cent of that dollar on selling. When one looks at the ratio of detail men to doctors-I heard it was ten to one and later that it is eight to one-it is quite clear that it is a higher ratio than in any other industry in Canada. This suggests that there are a great many ways in which to lay a framework or ground rules so that we will have a more competitive industry and one which will lead to lower costs. Therefore I do not believe that the argument concerning research is one that carries any weight when we consider the facts. The drug industry and one of its principal spokesmen in the House of Commons, the junior member for Halifax, have used this red herring.
The evidence presented before the special committee on drug costs and prices is to the contrary. It indicates that it is measures such
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act as the government's fiscal policy, the policy of the Department of Industry and the clinical testing required by the regulations of the food and drug directorate which have encouraged the little research we have had in Canada. Therefore the argument does not hold water. I should also like to point out that Canadian patents are overwhelmingly owned by foreigners who in the past have found it more efficient to concentrate their research activities elsewhere. The modest increase in research in Canada has been due to government policy and the clinical testing required by the food and drug directorate. This is the reason, and it should not be confused with the existing patent laws.
It has been mentioned also that research is socially desirable. I believe we all agree with that, but if we bear in mind the evidence given by the industry before the royal commission and before the special committee of the House of Commons we find there are other ways in which to encourage research. I disagree that that is the choice. I do not accept the premise that it boils down to the choice of the small amount of research we have justifying the high cost of drugs. I believe that the changes proposed by this legislation and the other steps which the government is taking and will take can lay the ground rules and framework for this industry to achieve the laudable goal of lower prices without affecting the small amount of research which is now carried on. I thank hon. members, Mr. Speaker, and will conclude my remarks very shortly. I have already said that when patents have been removed we have seen instances of lower drug prices.
The third part of the program is the provision to doctors, through the information services of the Department of National Health and Welfare, of objective material on various competing drugs that are on the market. Understandably, I think, doctors are very cautious in prescribing new drugs. Under the present system it is the drug industry, through its detail men, that does the selling. I believe that the dissemination of this type of information by an impartial agency will be very helpful and will give more leeway to doctors inasmuch as they will have more information on which to act. I think that in part at least this should deal with the very difficult problem of the 30 per cent of the cost of manufacturing drugs that is taken up with sales and marketing. I believe this figure is far too high and is a result of inefficiency. Quite clearly there is a responsibility on parliament to adopt measures to remedy the situation. I feel that the proposal regarding the information services branch of the department is a step in the right direction.
The minister also made reference to a fourth measure, the provision of certain assistance to some of the smaller Canadian manufacturers. The fifth matter was distribution, and the minister has indicated that he will be discussing this question with the provinces.
As I say, I do not think we can look to any one single measure to be entirely effective in solving the problems. However, I urge hon. members to support the legislation before the house. I suggest very strongly that the picture has become confused in the minds of some because research has been related to patents. When the evidence is examined this contention just does not stand up.
The second area of confusion has arisen because patents have been related to safety. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) asked a question of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) last night

which I thought was very pertinent. According to the evidence that he had found and which I also found-I do not have it with me right now but I will send it to the hon. member for Halifax-there is strong support for the argument that we should not confuse patents and safety.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that it seems that the opponents of this bill have no argument on which to base their case. They seem to be fearful of the effect on research, but I think the body of the evidence is against this. As an alternative it is a very costly price to pay. It seems to me there are other measures that stimulate research. The other argument the opposition has raised about safety has been dealt with by the minister and it will undoubtedly be dealt with by others.

Mr. Speaker, it has been interesting to listen to the amazing speech of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin). He accused us of using emotional arguments to call attention to some of the deficiencies in this bill. He seemed to think that the question of safety was not important enough to underline the fact that we feel some provisions have been left out of the legislation. The hon. member spoke about red herrings. This government is very good at drawing red herrings across the path. It is said that this legislation will reduce the cost of drugs, Mr. Speaker. But how much more welcome would be measures that would reduce the cost of living right across the board, or measures that would remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
Last year quite an issue was made of the fact that the sales tax on drugs was removed. However, on January 1 of this year a 5 per cent surcharge on income tax was imposed. And so on it goes, Mr. Speaker. Talk about red herrings. Sometimes I wonder whether this bill is not a red herring that has been brought in by the minister as a sort of sermon on the mount designed to move him ahead in the leadership campaign that is given such prominent publicity in the country today. I expect that the parliamentary secretary who has just spoken hopes to step into the minister's shoes some day and it could be that these speeches were prepared in anticipation of that event.
The effect of this bill as I see it is to allow the commissioner of patents to grant licences permitting the importation of prescription drugs on a more flexible basis than applies at
February 13, 1968	COMMONS
present. Where there is a delay in the granting by the commissioner of the required licence for a period beyond six months, provision is made for the granting of an interim licence under a patent relating to medicine.
On December 15 last, as reported at page 5467 of Hansard, the minister indicated that the objective of this bill was to allow compulsory licences to import prescription drugs, Which would have the effect of injecting more competition at the manufacturers' level in the drug industry and would beneficially affect the prices of drugs. In this connection it is rather interesting to look at the evidence given before the committee. On Tuesday, February 7, 1967, the committee received evidence from Mr. Henry, the director of investigation and research of the combines investigation branch. In connection with the competition that the minister feels is going to be injected into the industry as a result of this legislation the director of the combines investigation branch had this to say, as reported on page 2185 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence:
Price competition during the life of the patent is found only in limited circumstances, notably in sales to institutions and governments. Instead, competition takes the form of product differentiation which requires inordinately large sums to be spent on promotion of a particular firm's product, usually by its brand name, primarily to the physicians who make the selection at the time of prescribing for the patient. Competition is therefore cost increasing rather than price reducing. The more intense the competition, the higher costs are driven. There being no downward pressure on price there is no downward pressure on cost with the result that pressures within the firm for more detail men, more advertising, etc., tend to be inflationary, and resulting high costs are used to justify high prices.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We were pleased to note the aims that the minister has in connection with this legislation. They were stated in his speech yesterday and were: lower prices for drugs, safe drugs for the Canadian people and a viable Canadian drug industry. From evidence taken before the committee we know that increased competition does not always have the effect of reducing the price of a particular article that is being sold. Nevertheless, anything that can be done to bring about a reduction in the price of prescription drugs will win the wholehearted approval of members of the house and the public at large.
As a result of this legislation we are likely to witness the importation into Canada, under
DEBATES	6679
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act interim licences in many instances, of a whole range of pharmaceutical products bearing brand names that are identical or similar to those of Canadian products which have undergone testing and inspection at the government level. This problem arises. What assurance will Canadians have that these products bearing identification similar to that of Canadian products have passed the same tests as products made in this country? This bill, so far as I can see, provides only that the food and drug directorate shall be notified of any application to bring into Canada a pharmaceutical product from another country. Does the minister feel that mere notification from one department to another is sufficient? Surely drugs imported from other countries and purporting to possess the same qualities as drugs manufactured in Canada should be subjected to exactly the same testing conditions and requirements as drugs which are manufactured in Canada.
The question of safety in the use of drugs is not merely academic. There have been numerous instances in the past few years which have indicated that, despite all possible precautions, horrible consequences can arise unless drugs meet the most rigorous conditions as to manufacturing standards. The other day some children in Ottawa ate some candy which it was thought was injurious. After careful study it was found that the candy was not the cause of the trouble. But how certain are we that the sort of thing exemplified by this candy incident could not arise with regard to drugs? If we are now to open the door to an influx of drugs over whose manufacture Canadian authorities have no control, then surely we must take steps at this end to see to it that reasonable testing procedures are followed.
No doubt the minister will recall the recommendations of the House of Commons special committee on drug costs and prices in this regard. I now wish to refer to two recommendations made by that committee which have not, I am sorry to say, been incorporated into the legislation. Recommendation No. 17 reads as follows:
That subsection 3 of section 41 of the Patent Act be amended to indicate clearly that the granting of a licence by the commissioner of patents is subject to a report by the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare, to the effect that the applicant for the compulsory licence has satisfied the directorate that he has met the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act:

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
Recommendation No. 18 reads as follows:
That subsection 3 of section 41 of the Patent Act be amended to include applications for compulsory licences to import drug products in all forms, subject to inspection of manufacturing facilities by the food and drug directorate and provided such importation is in the public interest as may be determined by the commissioner; and to this end, your committee recommends that the rules under the Patent Act be amended to permit the commissioner to seek and receive outside independent expert advice in the determination of this question;
As I said, these two important recommendations by the committee do not seem to have been incorporated into this legislation. At least, there is nothing in the bill to show that these recommendations have been followed. Surely there is a responsibility on the government and on parliament to see to it that Canadians are granted an adequate level of protection. Drugs are not in the same category as other important materials. In a wide range of cases the assurance of effectiveness can mean that a person will live instead of dying, that a person will recover instead of suffering permanent and irretrievable damage. To put it succinctly, this is not an area to fool around in.
It is interesting to find that in the past there has been evidence of a little fooling around with regard to the question of safety of drugs and importation of drugs from foreign countries. This is substantiated by the evidence which was submitted before the special committee on drug costs and prices. Mr. Chapman, a witness before the committee, was questioned by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) about a report which appeared in Maclean's review of January 1, 1966. The hon. member for Verdun read a portion of that report to the witness, as found on page 2233 of the committee evidence:
The raw material from abroad is often processed and packaged by Canadian distributers lacking adequate knowhow on quality control.
A little farther on the hon. member for Verdun continued reading from the report as follows:
One example: An F.D.D. inspector found a kitchen table manufacturer putting out a drug which lost its potency within two days compared with the six-month's shelf life of the same drug producted by a reputable company. He just did not know how to stabilize it, the inspector explained. All too often these small operators simply don't know what they are doing.
As I said, the hon. member for Verdun was reading from an article in Maclean's review of January. Farther along in the evidence, 
replying to the hon. member for Verdun Mr. Chapman said:
Well, I might say sir, with regard to the first paragraph at the top of the third column, where it states:-
Then Mr. Chapman reads a few words from the report:
"Italy and Poland were recently removed from the UJK.'s list of suppliers in antibiotics."
Mr. Chapman then continued his own evidence by saying:
We still import pharmaceutical material from both countries. In Italy the laws call for manufacturers to assay their own products, but F.D.D. inspectors often find the test equipment dust-covered and obviously unused.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, safety in drug imports is not an area that should be fooled around in. I ask the minister whether he will entertain an amendment to the bill to ensure that not only will the commissioner of patents forward a copy of any notice of application to the food and drug directorate but that a full clinical and chemical description of the product, along with a sample for testing, will be forwarded at the same time. Needless to say, since I am not a medical man I am subject to correction on this point, but we should not ignore what the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) said yesterday in this regard. One would certainly like to hear the views of qualified medical men on the importation into Canada of drugs bearing brand names similar to those of Canadian products manufactured under the most rigid controls, since the imported varieties are manufactured under conditions which in some cases are known only to those who produce the drugs.
Most members of the committee-I know I did-received letters and information from people who are, of course, interested in the drug business. One important matter mentioned in that material was drug safety. Canadian drug manufacturers have operated with an enviable record of efficiency, safety and reliability for many years. The Department of National Health and Welfare, through the food and drug directorate, is in close and constant touch with those who manufacture drugs in this country. But what guarantee is there in the case of imported material originating we know not where? Another important point is that the country from which the material is imported may not be the country of origin.

[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
What is to stop the entry into the pharmaceutical stream of dangerous or even toxic products when there is an almost complete absence of controls? This is not to say there will be no controls, but there will be no assurance that the controls are present in every case or even as to the nature or extent of such controls as may exist. I ask the minister to give serious thought to this matter in order to avoid the horrible tragedies to which Canadians and many thousands who live in other countries have been subjected in the past. With new drugs coming on the market every day and with each new discovery bringing a rush of imitators, it is difficult to control the situation in Canada. Once you open the door to unrestricted and unregulated importation, in many cases from unknown sources, there will not be enough civil servants on the government payroll to undertake an inventory of pharmaceutical imports.
I call attention to the evidence given before the committee to the effect that applications submitted to the commissioner had to wait many months before they could be processed. One of the recommendations made by the committee, to which in my view considerable importance attaches, reads as follows:
That the personnel and facilities of the food and drug directorate be expanded to make possible the implementation of the recommendations of the Boyd committee, the Hilliard committee and this committee.
I maintain there is a need to incorporate into this legislation provisions dealing specifically with safety measures. Canadians are entitled to protection and surely the minimum protection to which they are entitled from this or any government is to know that when they buy drugs in Canada some attempt has been made to ensure that in seeking a cure or remedy they will not be doing themselves serious harm or injury. My own feeling is that if a system for testing and inspecting imported products cannot be worked out, then they should not be allowed into Canada. I ask the minister: Would he himself be prepared to take or allow his family to take such a harmless drug as aspirin if brought in from outside Canada and manufactured under conditions of which we knew nothing? I am sure he would have serious reservations. What then of drugs whose effects are more serious and potentially more harmful? Are Canadians not to have the assurance of government protection when it comes to the reliability of such preparations?
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
This is why I ask the minister to see that a provision is included in the measure before us requiring that with each import application a complete description and a sample for testing must be forwarded to Ottawa, and that no licence be granted until a clean bill of health in the form of a certificate is secured from the Department of National Health and Welfare. I do not think we can be too careful in dealing with considerations of human health. Human beings are not guinea pigs, though I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare did refer to the people of Canada on one occasion as acting as guinea pigs over a period of time until there had been an opportunity to examine particular products.
I do not know whether the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Turner) has consulted the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) on this point. If he has not, perhaps he will do so. I hope and trust that he has consulted the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, particularly those in the food and drug directorate, for the benefit and protection of Canadians. I am sure that if he has obtained the view of his officials the Minister of National Health and Welfare must look askance at a procedure which has the effect of breaking down safeguards laboriously erected over the years for the protection of our people. I appeal to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to look into the possibility of incorporating into this legislation measures which will ensure to all Canadians the best and the safest drugs possible.

Mr. Speaker, the problem we are tackling today has concerned the people of Canada for at least ten years. It is almost ten years since the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission was asked to look into the field of prescription drugs and the possibility of monopoly control existing in Canada in this important industry.
The commission reported that the price of drugs was too high. One of the examples given in its report tabled in 1961 was chlor-promazine, perhaps the most commonly used tranquilizer. It had been researched and developed in France and it was selling in Paris in that year for 77 cents while it was being retailed in Toronto for $6.25 for the same amount and the same strength.
We have had a report from the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. We have had a
February 13, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act report from the royal commission on health services under Mr. Justice Hall, appointed by the former Conservative government, and we have in our hands a report from a parliamentary committee which has held innumerable meetings on this subject.
I have been amazed at the contributions made by the three speakers so far for the official opposition, the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall), and the hon. member for Wellington-Huron (Mr. Howe). If there is one thing which is obvious it is that they have ignored completely the advice given to the government and the committee by the head of the anti-combines branch, Mr. Henry. They have ignored completely the advice given by the head of the food and drug administration, Dr. Chapman. They have ignored completely the advice given by doctors who direct the operations of the largest hospitals in Canada. They have ignored completely the recommendations and the advice of the auditors appointed by the committee who found that the prices charged by Canadian drug manufacturers are too high. What they have told us could have been-I am not saying it was-written by the paid representatives of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. Every word of it.

It is not good enough lor us on this side of the house or for the Canadian people to save a few pennies, without measuring value and the safety of the users of the drug. Surely, that is poor business sense.

chief executive officer in the federal drug administration, the man responsible for the safety of drugs, had to say in this connection. I want to deal with another point, generic drugs. From what has been said one would think there would be great danger if the people of Canada were permitted to purchase prescription drugs under their generic names. I am not a doctor, like the hon. member for Simcoe East, but the facts are very plain. We heard the evidence again and again before the committee. I am sure the hon. member for Simcoe East cannot and would not dispute what I am going to say.
There is not a hospital in Canada, whether it be the Royal Victoria in Montreal, the Winnipeg General or the Toronto Sick Children's, which, when it fills prescriptions for people who are really sick-I think it is fair to assume that people in hospital are sicker than people who visit doctors in their offices and take prescriptions to their local druggists -uses brand name drugs. There is not a doubt that the vast bulk of prescriptions filled in Canadian hospitals are filled under the supervision and direction of the best doctors in Canada. So far as I know it is the doctors on the teaching staffs of medical schools who usually staff the big teaching hospitals. They

use generic name drugs, some of which are manufactured and some of which are imported into Canada.
I do not think the hon. member for Simcoe East would want this house and the people of Canada to believe for one moment that the doctors directing Canadian hospitals would order prescription drugs under generic names if they were not certain those drugs were adequate, up to a high standard and safe to use. When people talk about the use of generic drugs and warn the public that they are dangerous, I say they are creating a red herring. Consciously or unconsciously they are trying to protect the profit position of the large drug companies in this country.
This bill, when passed, will give legislative effect to some of the large number of recommendations made by the special committee of the House of Commons which dealt with drug costs and prices. It is true that not all its recommendations are being implemented. All during the committee hearings I for one agreed that the food and drug directorate must be given sufficient manpower and money so that every drug which is sold in Canada can be certified safe by the government. I do not care whether a drug is cheap or expensive. If it is not safe it ought not to be used in Canada, it ought not to be prescribed in Canada, it ought not to be sold in Canada. I do not think the government is doing enough in this respect and when we reach the departmental estimates I certainly intend to urge that the drug inspection service be expanded. But that has nothing to do with the bill which we are discussing today. This bill has nothing to do with generic drugs.
The most important change that the bill will make, if passed, is covered in that part of it which deals with trade marks. The bill will permit the importation of brand name drugs, trade mark drugs, if this is thought worth while from a price point of view. What would this mean? I suggest to the hon. member for Simcoe East that he look at the committee's report. He was a member of the committee, but I refer him to the details of its report. I refer the hon. member to page 80 which gives actual examples of the prices of drugs in this country and their prices in other countries. Here I am not talking about generic name drugs but about brand name drugs. Chloromecytin, produced by the Parke, Davis Company, the very drug which the hon. member for Simcoe East was asking questions

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act about during question period today, sells in Canada for $23.64 per 100 tablets. In London, England, the price is $11.18. Under this bill, if a drug wholesaler wants to import Parke, Davis Chloromycetin from Great Britain he will be able to buy it there, pay the duty on it, pay the freight, and bring it into Canada more cheaply than he could buy it from Parke, Davis in Canada, with the result that he will be able to offer it to retail druggists at a lower price and that lower price will be passed on to the consumer. That is what the hon. member for Simcoe East wants to oppose.

Warner-Lambert is not some fly by night company; it is one of the giants of the United States pharmaceutical industry. I refer to another story which appeared in a labour union publication on June 4, 1966. This is what the article had to say:
More than a third of the nation's drug makers are violating U.S. rules on false and misleading advertising. That startling disclosure came from the head of the food and drug administration, Dr. James L. Goddard. He told a house subcommittee hearing, that these violations include distortion of claims for usefulnesses, misinforming the doctor on the size of the drug test, claims of no side effects despite test evidence to the contrary and failure to modify old ads when new research indicated their message was invalid.
I am sorry the hon. member for Simcoe East has left the chamber because I wanted to indicate that one of the most flagrant violations in respect of failure to give the real information to doctors was perpetrated by the very company in respect of the very drug to which he referred, namely, Parke, Davis and Chloromycetin. I have put these quotations on the record for two reasons, first, because I want the record to show very clearly that the large drug manufacturers and members of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association do not have a completely clean bill of health and, second, because they demonstrate conclusively the contention of some of us, including members of the official opposition on the committee, that we ought not leave the health and welfare of Canadians to the tender mercies of individual drug companies which have their own axes to grind and are interested -I am not critical in this regard because this is how the free enterprise system works-in making a profit. We ought to assure that the food and drug administration of Canada is given the responsibility and takes on the job of making certain that the people of Canada get safe drugs. On that basis I can agree with the hon. member for Halifax. However, that is not the issue here today. The issue is
February 13, 1968

whether this bill will help bring down the price of prescription drugs to Canadian consumers.
The hon. member for Halifax was correct when he said that this bill does not do all the things the committee said it should do. Of course it does not. One of the things the committee said should be done was the removal of the 12 per cent sales tax on prescription drugs. That was accomplished months ago. There are other things which will be done, as I mentioned earlier, by various branches of government, including the food and drug directorate. The bill is a direct result of recommendation No. 21 of the special committee to be found at page 54 of the committee's report. I commend it to the hon. member for Halifax for examination. This is what it says:
That section 20 of the Trade Marks Act be amended to make clear that no infringement can be claimed where imported drugs are manufactured by a "related" company;-
We have heard a great deal from hon. members about the dangers of unrestricted importation as a result of products being brought in from Great Britain, for example, which might not be the same as those sold in Canada under the same brand name. I find it hard to believe that the hon. member for Halifax and the hon. member for Simcoe East really believed what they were saying. If they did they must believe that there is a difference between the brand name products or prescription drugs made by Parke, Davis, Warner-Chilcott, Eli, Lilly, Lederle or American Cyanamid in Great Britain and those made by the same companies in Canada. I have too much respect for these international drug companies to believe for one minute that achromycin, Chloromycetin, gantrisin, equanil and enovid made in Great Britain are different from the same products made in Canada or different from the same drugs produced in various other countries of the world under the same brand name. I am sure these drugs meet the same standards whether they are made in Great Britain, France, Italy, Canada or the United States. Yet that was the implication of what those hon. members were saying. I suggest that it is nonsense.
We have heard a great deal about selective choices. I think I should very briefly put on the record what the witnesses did say about drugs and drug practices. I refer hon. members to the second and final report of the special committee of the House of Commons
27053-421J
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act on drug costs and prices. Let me quote a few sentences from page 12:
The committee believes that the profits of pharmaceutical companies in Canada appear about twice as high as the level of profits of the manufacturing industry as a whole.
These are the poor defenceless people the hon. member for Simcoe East attempted to defend last evening. He said this bill would take the bread from their mouths; they were going to be cast into perdition and would have to go out of business. This is what the committee said:
The committee is not concerned primarily with reducing profit below a reasonable level but it is concerned with reducing costs of drugs to the consumer. The committee is convinced that this can be done within the framework of the free enterprise system.

In fact, one of the conclusions reached by the director was that "prices of drugs in Canada are among the highest in the world."
I commend that sentence to the junior member for Halifax who suggested that we were talking about saving only pennies for the Canadian consumer. The report goes on to say:
Thirdly, more up to date figures on the comparison of prices of drugs in Canada with those in other countries having relatively advanced economies were presented to the committee by the Consumers' Association of Canada. These figures likewise substantiated the conclusions of the Green Book.
Farther on in the report the committee said:
Your committee confirms the previous findings now on public record; and it has come to the inescapable conclusion that drug prices in Canada are in fact high and that every fair and reasonable step should be taken to reduce these prices.
The junior member for Halifax was a member of the committee and I presume he endorsed this report when it was prepared. Lord knows, some of us wanted a strong report and the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), will confirm that we spent many hours twice

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act a week over a period of weeks reaching agreement with members like the junior member for Halifax and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand), who wanted to be 200 per cent certain that the committee report did not say anything which might hurt anybody unfairly. It is apparent from Table 1-

-that the operating results for 1961-1964 do not indicate any material change in trend from that shown for the period 1953-1960, dealt with by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. This is one of the highest profit industries in the country, an industry to whose defence the hon. member for Halifax and other members of the official opposition spring. The table shows that for the years 1953 to 1963, a ten year period and a pretty good period to consider, the percentage return on capital investment in the pharmaceutical industry was 19.71 compared with just 10.40 for all manufacturing companies. For pharmaceutical companies, for the years 1958 to 1963 the average return was 13.77 per cent while for all manufacturing it was just 7.42 per cent. Again, drug manufacturers are making almost twice as much money as other companies.
February 13, 1968

I want to repeat what I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, and I shall close on this note. I showed, as did the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) yesterday and on several other occasions, from the records compiled by the experts employed by the committee the tremendous difference in the prices charged in various countries for prescription drugs. I did not deal just with the difference in price between brand name drugs and generic drugs because this is not the time or place to discuss that question. I dealt with the difference in the prices of brand name drugs as between Canada and other countries. One can look at the prices charged in London, Paris, Bern, Switzerland; Rome, Italy; Bonn, Germany and the United States and one will see that the only country in which the prices of prescription drugs are as high or higher than in Canada is the United States. I demonstrated earlier that in Great Britain brand name drugs are sold for half the price they are in this country, or even less. Who is paying these exorbitantly high prices? As the hon. member for St. John's (Mr. Cashin) said, it is the consumer who pays them; it is the poor working man, whether he lives in Halifax, Simcoe East, Winnipeg, Toronto or Vancouver.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Some persons find it necessary to take a drug such as equanil three times a day over a period of weeks or months. If a doctor prescribes equanil the patient may have to pay as much as ten cents for a tablet. When we speak of a person earning $50, $60 or $70 a week having to pay 30 cents a day for a prescription drug we are not talking about a luxury; we are talking about the kind of circumstances where a family would have to make do with one less quart of milk per day.
This is the reason that I, like the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin), was so surprised at the contribution of the junior member for Halifax. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who must have prescriptions filled every week, whether they be for tranquilizers, sedatives or antibiotics, and what is involved is an expenditure which frequently amounts to $5 or $10 per prescription.
I am sure that every member of parliament over the years has received many letters from his constituents asking him to do something about this situation. They say they simply cannot afford to pay these high prices. These people are particularly disturbed when they read the profit figures published occasionally
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act by the drug companies because these figures show the fantastic profits of these companies. They write to their members and probably to the minister asking that something be done. Finally the government has acted. Finally we have one part of the package that was suggested by the committee.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the report of the committee contained every recommendation it should have. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman), I believe the best way in which to do something about the price of prescription drugs would be for the government to establish a crown corporation which would manufacture and distribute certain important and basic prescription drugs. It is the doctors of Canada who decide what prescriptions will be written which the pharmacists in the hospitals and in the drug stores across Canada will fill. As a group they write hundreds of thousands of prescriptions a day. Therefore, if we had such a crown corporation we could save the people of Canada tens of millions of dollars a year.
Unfortunately the government has not made such a proposal. I do not expect the minister will ever make such a proposal even if he and I are here for the next 30 years, because I do not think he would consider that kind of solution. However, the legislation before us today is a step in the right direction. It contains one of a whole battery of proposals made by the committee in an effort to bring down the prices of prescription drugs. I hope this legislation will be passed and go into effect very quickly. Although I suppose I am hoping for the impossible I hope that the members of the official opposition will reconsider the impossible position they have taken during the past couple of days. I do not wish to be unfair but I say they are taking a position which can bring comfort only to a very small group of Canadians, namely, the members of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. I hope that we can complete the discussion of this bill in all stages in the next couple of days, pass it unanimously, and get on with the overdue task of seeing that drug prescriptions are filled at a reasonable cost.

I must remind the hon. member that it is a Liberal government that introduced Bill No. C-190 which will certainly bring about a reduction of drug prices in Canada. This measure had been anticipated for 40 years, and I am very glad that the hon. member was thoughtful enough to thank the government for having at last introduced it.
I hope I will be permitted to take a few very precious minutes to make my humble contribution to consideration of Bill No. C-190, which will bring about, as I have just mentioned, with the legislation already passed, a substantial reduction of drug prices to consumers.
As an answer to the eloquent testimony of my colleagues in opposition and to the arguments which have been put forward, I wish to quote the following Japanese proverb: If you understand everything, you are badly informed. It is impossible to understand everything.
First of all, it is essential to understand that the drug industry cannot be considered in the same way as all the other industries in 1968. It is an industry which belongs to a public service called health, a blessing unequalled by any other on earth. As I said, this service belongs in part to the public sector, and therefore it is up to the government to take the steps necessary to normalize the excessive profits of this important-and I would even say privileged-industry by modifying the Patent Act in such a way as to allow competition in order to bring about a considerable reduction in drug prices. I think that is the whole essence of the bill.
Dealing with the normalization of profits, I find it shameful and scandalous that drug companies realize up to 27.25 per cent profit from their investments, while all the other manufacturing enterprises get an average of 13.25 per cent, according to 1959 figures. It is also scandalous to see that certain companies have spent up to 50 per cent of their annual budget on publicity and that, in 1964, for instance, 34 companies have spent $35 million in this field. On the other hand, it is hypocritically advocated that the Canadian drug industry-to be more exact, I should say 35 drug companies-has spent $9,551,000 in 1960 on research, namely 8.3 per cent of the total amount of their sales. However, what the drug industry is not saying is that it has, in fact, spent only a third of this sum, in Canada that is, $3,349,000, leaving to the headquarters of the drug companies the huge sum of 
DEBATES	February 13, 1968
$6,202,000, subscribed to their research fund although research work was done outside Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this borders on legal fraud, and I hope that the Department of National Revenue, in conjunction with the Departments of Industry and Defence Production, will take the necessary steps to check the drain of Canadian dollars or recover the sums spent by our sick when buying very expensive drugs. The money thus spent could contribute to national production or be considered as taxable capital. Since the Canadian drug companies spend an insignificant amount on research, they should, in my opinion, be made to spend the money received by their headquarters for research, in order to find a way to reduce the cost of drugs.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The drug industry in Canada makes a lot of its research through false devices which are only a publicity screen to increase its profits.
I do not need to add that the drug industry in Canada is only a subsidiary of the American drug industry which owns nine tenths of our so-called Canadian industry.
We have often heard in Canada about rackets or combines in the drug industry. It has even been implied that every Canadian physician was getting up to $5,000 of advertising literature. In fact, most medical magazines are subsidized by the drug companies and they are often filled, from cover to cover, with colour photographs representing everything that the fertile imagination of publicity agents can think of to praise this or that drug. But what has that to do with the quality, the therapeutic effect of those drugs? It is false representations for a magazine to show a beautiful smiling woman, hardly dressed, merely wrapped in a wonderful oriental-coloured piece of material.
Doctors are deluged with samples. There is systematic brain-washing, always in terms of a given article. That is why the Harley committee recommended that a national formulary should be published to enable doctors to choose themselves the drug to be prescribed.
It has been claimed with great fuss that the Food and Drug Directorate was not up to the task, that, after the passage of this new legislation, its staff and the number of inspections-would have to be increased.
I think that the government has done its best since it has increased the number of inspectors in that department from 93 in 1962
February 13, 1968	COMMONS
to approximately 200 at the present time, that is a percentage of 50 per cent. Canadians will certainly be protected, since the government has undertaken to improve its Food and Drug Directorate which is, by the way, recognized as one of the best in the world, according to Professor Blanc, a world authority in pharmacology, a professor at Geneva University and a member of the World Health Organization.
Now, nobody should try to make us believe that our Food and Drug Directorate is not working properly. I maintain that it is the best in the world, as stated by a competent member of the World Health Organization in Geneva.
For the information of those who are still not convinced, I will say that the number of inspections made by the Food and Drug Directorate gradually increased from 242 in 1963 to 551 in 1966. On November 8, 1967 the Canadian Medical Association sent to the minister a resolution it had adopted and which said:

This committee recommends that the Canadian Medical Association make known its views to the Registrar General that we are in favour of measures which will reduce drug costs to the patient but that these reduced costs must not be at the expense or safety of drugs or at the expense of retarding the continuing growth of the Canadian drug industry.

In this resolution signed by its executive secretary, the association states clearly that it favours measures likely to lower drug prices but is against certain measures that will lower the quality and safety of drugs. The Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) answered as follows:

It would be wrong to suggest that there is any degree of uncertainty concerning safety of imported drugs.

I must add that a patent has nothing to do with the quality of a drug. Quality control depends exclusively, first, on the Food and Drug Directorate, a branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and secondly, on the manufacturer's integrity. There has never been any evidence that the quality of a drug was lessened at the expiration of a patent. This brings me to deal briefly with generic drugs.
Even though the Department of National Defence and a very great number of Canadian
DEBATES	6689
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act hospitals have been buying, for a long time, huge quantities of generic drugs, and always with a view to reducing the price of those drugs, their use has never given rise to serious difficulties. As I said, it is quite definite that the government will increase the number of its inspectors in order to guarantee that all drugs coming from Europe or elsewhere will satisfy the standards prescribed by the Food and drug Directorate. This is quite a small price to pay if one considers the great benefit which will derive from this for those who must take drugs but cannot because of the high price of drugs in 1968. I must add here that the officials of the Food and Drug Directorate have been very clear in their evidence and that, according to their views, based on an analysis made by inspectors, the generic drug and the brand name drug provide the same guarantees as to their quality and security. This can be found on page 12 of the Harley report.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Having said this, I should like to make a small digression to philosophize a bit on drugs and to demonstrate that the policy adopted by our government is the best with regard to lower prices, since it takes into account the underprivileged class, the sick and the handicapped, and this is beyond value. Since 1900, and I now refer to an article from the Women's Medical News which appeared in the Montreal La Presse last August, the life expectancy of the American woman has been extended by 25 years. She can hope to live to be 73 while the average man will not reach 70 years of age.
From 1920 to this day, woman's life expectancy has increased by 19 years. Since 1920, thanks to drugs discovered in recent years, humanity benefits from what I shall call "a living bonus". Those "living bonus" years are more than added pages to one's calendar. They are productive, pleasant to live, and not only do they spare human lives but they also spare human beings from handicaps or reduced physical activity.
The invalid's bed and the wheelchair are becoming increasingly rare, which led a research specialist to say: We do not only add years to life expectancy, we add life to each year lived. Ten years ago, 80 per cent of the drugs prescribed today did not exist. As you know, the new drugs relieve arthritis, schizophrenia, pain, and allergies; perhaps that is why members can make speeches. These new drugs cure pneumonia, rheumatic fever, tuberculosis and venereal disease.
6690	COMMONS
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
New vaccines can inoculate little girls against infantile paralysis and measles. In a few months, we will have a vaccine against the mumps. And we can expect to have a vaccine against German measles within two to five years. Yet about a decade ago, these illnesses seemed to be the common lot of all children, threatening them with possible blindness, disability and deafness. All that goes to show that we must, at all costs, find the means, as I said earlier, to lower drug prices, for when we get to a certain age, which I will call a "living bonus", that is to say years added to our life span by medical science, we can no longer afford to stay in good health, often because we do not have the financial means, or because of limited financial means, and mostly because of the high price of drugs.
It is well known that, when we get beyond a certain age, the number of prescriptions we use undergoes a noticeable yearly increase, due to the fact that we must often maintain our physical health by the use of new and efficient drugs. We must therefore protect this group of people to whom we have given this "living bonus" through our modern medical discoveries, our social security and preventive medicine programs. Through this legislation, we could add a supplement to this "living bonus".
It must be noted that this bill is practically a statement of principles to create fair competition which will lead to an administrative program designed to set the price of drugs at a level everyone can afford. It is to be hoped that the Canadian drug industry will recognize that this legislation is justified and that it will take this opportunity to reduce the price of drugs in the near future. If they are intelligent-and they have proved it in their brief-the drug people will recognize that the best competition is still the one that can be avoided.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with earlier speakers that this is a very complicated and important piece of legislation. This much was indicated by the minister sponsoring Bill No. C-190, because he required almost an hour and a half to explain all its ramifications. He made a well prepared presentation on behalf of his department in defence of his proposed action to allow easier entrance of foreign produced drugs into Canada.

DEBATES	February 13. 1968
To make my position clear, Mr. Speaker, I want to state at the outset, and state emphatically, that I support the intended effect of the bill, which is to make drug prices in Canada as reasonable as possible. I emphasize the words "intended effect of the bill", because what might be considered short term benefits might not in turn produce long term benefits to drug purchasers, drug manufacturers or to the economy of Canada as a whole. Proper legislative enactments to provide drugs at reasonable prices for all Canadians, particularly the elderly and low income groups, will certainly receive my support and I am sure will receive the support of my colleagues on this side of the house. I have received letters from constituents in connection with the present prices of drugs and I have assured the writers that we on this side of the house will do all in our power to see that prices are set at reasonable levels. I should like to repeat the statement I just made. We want to make sure that proper pricing methods are followed and that proper legislative enactments are passed to achieve the desired results. Again I emphasize the word "proper". Perhaps we might make some improvements to the bill before it finally passes.
I was a part time member only of the special committee on drug costs and prices. I had to yield my place on that committee owing to the demands of the standing committee on transport and communications. Being on the committee for only a short time I therefore cannot speak with the authority of the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall), or the hon. member for Wellington-Huron (Mr. Howe) on all the testimony given before the committee. They have put their comments on the record and have made it clear that there are serious doubts that Bill No. C-190 will give definite assurance of long term benefits in the public interest. The hon. member for Wellington-Huron particularly emphasized the absolute necessity to ensure complete safety of all drugs that are made available to the public, especially those drugs that are imported. I will not take up the time of the house to repeat his warnings but I certainly want to bring this matter to the attention of those who will be voting on this bill later in the week.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I am mainly concerned about the words on the front page of the bill, "An Act to amend the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act." In
February 13, 1988

this connection I wish to read a short paragraph from a letter I received from the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada.
Bill C-190 essentially would abolish normal patent and some trade mark rights as they relate to prescription medicines made in Canada. It has far-reaching implications in that it represents a serious attack on the patent system, a fundamental facet of any competitive society and a matter of significance to the Canadian economy. We believe it might set an unfortunate precedent.
That paragraph emphasizes my concern about what appears to be a dangerous tampering with patent rights in Canada. I am not an expert on patents so I consulted Webster's international dictionary, third edition, and under "patent" I found the following definition:
A government grant of a monopoly right that gives one who invents or discovers a new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or a new and useful improvement thereof the exclusive right for a specific term of 17 years with certain rights of extension to make, use or sell his invention or discovery.
The bill refers to compulsory licensing, and in this regard I consulted the 1965 edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Though the paragraph refers to Great Britain, what it says has application in this country.
Since the original object of the patent laws was the establishment of new industries, the main grounds for a grant of a compulsory license are that the patented invention is not being worked within the country-
I underline the words "within the country", -to the fullest practicable extent, or that the demand is not being met on reasonable terms, or is being met by importation in place of home manufacture.
To be fair I must also read the following paragraph that appears in the Encyclopaedia Britannica:
Applications for compulsory licenses relating to food or medicine may be made at any time and without alleging abuse of monopoly. Such compulsory licenses are to be granted unless there is good reason for refusal, and are to be on such terms as will secure that the patented article shall be available to the public on the lowest terms consistent with fair remuneration to the patentee.
I cannot say too much about fair remuneration with regard to patents but, according to certain testimony presented to the committee by the controller of patents, I understand that in these cases the payment of royalties would amount to a mere pittance. From what I have heard and read and received by way of comment in letters and briefs, it seems to me that 27053-422
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act patent rights are an essential incentive to adequate pharmaceutical research in Canada. I hold no brief for the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, and I stress that. Some speakers have suggested that perhaps we are speaking on its behalf. I hold no brief for the association but it is not difficult to share its concern about the effect that Bill C-190, if passed in its present form, will have on future drug research and development in Canada. In its brief the association says:
Bill C-190, which would have the effect of abolishing patents, could never be considered conducive to "continued and increased scientific research in Canada."
The brief goes on to say:
Patents are generally recognized as having a twofold value. They provide an incentive to discovery and encourage the disclosure of scientific information from which other researchers benefit.
In this connection it is fitting to put on record the 1967-68 statement of policy of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. No doubt each member of the house received a copy of that document. In one of its pronouncements on policy the chamber of commerce said, as noted in the P.M.A.C. brief:
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in its 196768 statement of policy, has urged that the government "implement a review of the Patent Act with respect to its being strengthened so as to encourage research and invention in Canada."
The legislation now before us is based on the idea that Canada can get along without its pharmaceutical industry. I am concerned about that. If Canada becomes dependent on other countries for vital drug supplies as may happen if this bill passes, her national health could be impaired in times of emergency.
I shall put on the record the extent of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada as outlined in the brief from the association: Canada's pharmaceutical industry makes an appreciable and growing contribution to the national economy. It employs over 10,000 Canadians-of whom 2,500 are university graduates-and helps to create jobs for an estimated 25,000 more in firms providing supplies and services for the industry. The member companies of our Association have a total capital investment of nearly $100 million.
The brief goes on to say:
Their exports in 1966, as shown in a recent survey conducted jointly by the Department of Industry and the Association, amounted to some $20 million, a figure which these companies are continually striving to increase. The proposed legislation not only would put an end to any hopes of this export development, but would also further upset Canada's negative balance of payments.
February 13, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
I thought I should read those paragraphs into the record because they indicate the extent of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada.
With regard to research, I have just received a copy of the first edition of a pamphlet put out by the Canadian Association for the Advancement of Health Sciences. The pamphlet refers to medical research and health sciences, and I think the latter aspect also includes research in drugs. In one part the pamphlet says:
The publication of this bulletin for the benefit of those involved in medical research or interested in the improvement of the research environment in Canada is in response to a growing public and professional awareness of the importance of the health sciences which has been building up in recent years.
A few paragraphs farther on it says:
Unless a more favourable environment for medical research-
I include pharmaceutical research under this heading.
-is provided as a matter of urgency, the skilled manpower on which medical education and health care depend will be inadequate both in quantity and quality.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In this connection, perhaps I might refer briefly to something which appears in a booklet issued in January by the Department of National Health and Welfare. It contains an article entitled "Measuring Medication Costs" which includes a whole series of price indices, founded on 1949 as the base year. The writer states:
The drugs on the market in 1949 represented the standard of health care of that period. The price of these particular drugs over the years changed only slightly as shown by the consumer price index. Changes have occurred, however, in the drugs actually prescribed by physicians. Instead of using the same drugs as in 1949, physicians are now using many new "wonder drugs" which usually cost more than the older, more established products.
We are then given a list showing how prices have changed. The article goes on:
If physicians did not use any new drugs but continued to prescribe the same medication as in 1949 the average prescription price would have changed very little. Now we can ask the question, why do physicians prescribe new drugs?
The answer is that either the new products are better than the previously existing products or they control or they cure a disease for which there previously was no effective drug treatment. Within the last decade, for example, we have for the first time developed effective drugs to treat glaucoma, fungus infections, mental depression and high blood pressure. The treatment of other diseases has also improved through the introduction of new antibiotics, tranquilizers, vaccines and anti-cancer drugs.
[Mr. Pascoe.l

I quote from this article because I believe it is germane to the problem we are now facing. We are bound to be concerned about the new drugs which are becoming available and the cost of research necessary to produce them.
Perhaps I might return to the question of patents. Any abolition of a patent right tends in my opinion to create a perilous precedent which might make it easier to abrogate other rights. I have had some experience in connection with copyright and I believe these two fields are to a certain extent related. According to the Encyclopaedia Britannica "copyright" is a term currently used to designate the rights secured by the laws of civilized countries to authors of literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works to protect them against unauthorized copying of those works. To bring the situation closer to us, I suggest that tampering with patent rights could open up other areas such as copyright and make them liable to infringement. We have all heard statements at the end of National Hockey League, World Series baseball and Grey Cup games that they cannot be rebroadcast without authorization because there is a copyright protecting the original broadcast. I suggest that copyright and patent laws are in the same category and that changes made in one of these fields could over the years become the thin end of a wedge making it possible to introduce changes in the other.
Perhaps I should offer some suggestions to the minister for his consideration following these remarks on patents. I am sure this matter will be the subject of discussion during the clause by clause study in committee. It has been claimed that drug manufacturers are spending too much on the promotion and distribution of their products. The figure often quoted is 30 cents on the operating dollar. I certainly agree that this is a high figure and that it does add to the cost of drugs to the consumer.
I would remind hon. members that the committee which went into this subject recommended that the food and drug directorate issue a monthly publication to medical doctors outlining the effectiveness of all drugs available at that particular time and commenting on their safety and efficacy. I believe such a publication would be of great value. It would be official and authoritative and it would list all those drugs which the directorate considered to be most effective in particular cases. It would command the attention of
February 13, 1968

all doctors who prescribe medication for their patients. In my view the availability of such a publication would undoubtedly reduce the cost of promotion to pharmaceutical manufacturers. They would not have to use 30 cents of every dollar to advertise the new drugs which they have created through research. I suppose it would still be necessary to employ what they call detail men to call on doctors and talk to them. However, I believe a monthly publication outlining all these drugs would be of great assistance and would cut down the cost of drugs to the public.
I took down one quotation from the minister in the course of the hour and a half during which we listened to him yesterday. He said that during any given interval of time the incidence of disease was far from uniform and those who incurred the highest drug bills because of their disabilities were likely to have incomes substantially below the average.
I agree with this statement. I myself have been contacted by people who have had the greatest difficulty in paying for the drugs they need. In this connection I have a suggestion to make which the minister might well consider. Instead of taking action which would certainly curtail the operations of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada, I suggest that people with incomes substantially below the average should be given special consideration by the government. I am not proposing any form of means test in this connection. The government has taken the position that the plan they introduced for the payment of supplementary pensions to people with low incomes does not involve any form of means test or needs test.
My suggestion is that the minister propose to his colleagues in the government that those receiving supplementary pensions be provided with necessary drugs at minimum cost. Such a course would cost the government far less, in my opinion, than the revenue which would be lost in taxation if the pharmaceutical industry in Canada were curtailed or lost. Perhaps this proposal could be considered in more detail during the committee stage. In the meantime I leave it with the minister to ponder.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
