speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at great length this evening but I do wish to make some statement on Bill C-190. I think it very important that we as members of the House of Commons try to satisfy the insistent
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act demand that something be done about the high cost of drugs, but I have found the public to be singularly sceptical about our ability to affect drug prices. Members of the public point to the failure of the elimination of the sales tax on drugs to reduce their price to any degree.
There is a problem and it is important that we tackle it squarely and give the public the assurance that we have their best interests at heart. The discussions in the special committee have been referred to at length. One of the most interesting things in that committee was the story, repeated over and over again, of how Canadian drug companies had become wholly owned American subsidiaries owing to the tax policies of successive federal governments, particularly inheritance and death duty taxes. I expect that later this week we will be presented with a report on United States investment in Canada, but I am sure that report will not contain one chapter showing how the tax policies of Canadian governments provided the incentive and rationale for United States investment in Canada.
Those who weep now about the effect which this bill may have on the Canadian drug industry have not paid full attention to the testimony given to the standing committee. I draw the attention of hon. members specifically to the submission of the government of Alberta to that committee. I have no intention of reading it all but I am sure the chairman and the members of the standing committee recall it well. Indeed, one member of the committee remarked that it could well have a cover slapped on it and be handed in as the committee's report. I believe the Alberta submission was influential in the drafting of the committee's final report and influenced the minister's opening statement yesterday. I suggest that if the bill is passed and the minister is given a boost by it he will on occasion, on his travels across the country, give some credit to the submission of the government of Alberta.
Chapter 3 of the Alberta government's submission specifically relates to the bill we are considering. It deals with the influence of the legal and regulatory framework on Canadian drug prices and asks why the level of Canadian drug prices is the highest in the world. It lists several of the factors that influence drug prices, whether the drugs are manufactured
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act in Canada or imported into the country, and I quote some of these factors:
-presence or absence of process and product patents in the foreign country; tariffs, quotas, or other impediments to free foreign trade; presence or absence of price controls on drugs; the status of the existing drug industry in a given country, and similar factors.
I believe that by far the most important is patent policy, and it is not surprising that this bill deals with that aspect in an effort to provide some relief from the high cost of drugs. The Alberta submission goes on to say:
In Canada there are five major elements in the legal framework which influence the level of drug prices directly and indirectly.
It lists these as the patent and trade mark laws, tariffs and anti-dumping laws, the federal sales tax, the food and drug laws, and legal sanction for the practice of brand name prescribing. It goes on to say that the adoption of compulsory licensing in the United States would be of very great benefit to Canada but points out that this is not likely to happen. It adds:
The best solution would then seem to lie in the area of enabling those presently price competitive elements of the Canadian drug market-chiefly the small, Canadian-owned firms-to be able to compete more effectively with the major foreign patentholding firms. Measures should also be taken to induce new entry by price competitors. If about 90 per cent of the Canadian drug industry is presently controlled by firms which do not choose to take advantage of compulsory licensing, then steps should be taken to increase the viability of the existing competitive segment of the market, and to introduce new competition, if necessary from abroad, in the interest of lowering Canadian drug prices.
To that end the submission presented a variety of recommendations. It discussed the possibility of the complete abolition of drug patents but felt this would not be the wisest course for the government to take. Some of its recommendations were:
1.	Compulsory licences to import should be granted, subject to the payment of reasonable royalties.
Royalties still remain.
3.	Every effort should be made to further expedite the process of acting on compulsory licence applications-
4.	Section 19 of the Patent Act should be amended to allow provincial governments and their agencies as well as the government of Canada to use any patented drug, subject to the payment of reasonable compensation-
5.	The schedule of tariffs on drugs should be reviewed by the Tariff Board with a view toward:
(a) Limiting the liability of drugs to tariff duties to those drugs of a class or kind actually made in Canada-

February 13, 1968
It goes on to add:
7. Liability for anti-dumping duty should be limited to drugs of a kind actually made in Canada, where ''kind'' is defined in terms of the active ingredient.
It ends with this recommendation:
14. If the above reforms do not succeed in reducing drug prices to competitive levels in a reasonable period of time, drug patents in Canada should be completely abolished.
We who sat on the committee know that its report was considerably watered down. Some of us who attended all the committee hearings, and were particularly impressed with submissions such as the one from the Alberta government, had cause to wonder just how much we could give away, how much we could concede and still have a report left that would produce any noticeable affect on the price of drugs. I trust that the report was not watered down so as to be without effect. I trust that this legislation, in spite of what is being said by the official opposition, will prove of benefit to the public.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with a certain amount of trepidation to say a few words in connection

February 13, 19S8

with Bill C-190, which is before the house tonight, because on occasions during this debate hon. members of this party, when putting forward what I consider entirely reasonable points of view, have been harangued by hon. members opposite. I have in mind particularly the unwarranted and ungentlemanly outburst by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin). I am sorry he is not in the house at this moment.
The speech made by that hon. member did not do him credit, nor was it a credit to the decorum usually present in this house. I suggest that is exactly what he did. He tried to arouse hon. members of the house in respect of an emotional point in order to obscure the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall).
No one on this side of the house has made any pretence that the cost of drugs in this country is anything but high. No one has pretended that we would like to see anything but lower cost. We are all aware of the fact that drugs represent a very expensive commodity in this country. This is an item of cost that is felt particularly by those who can least afford to pay for them out of their budgets. I refer, of course, to the elderly and the sick. Naturally these people cannot afford to meet this expense at present pension levels.

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act in connection with one of the submissions to that committee. Although I do not know where it may be found in the committee proceedings, I have read a newspaper report based on it.

During the latest House of Commons committee investigation into drug costs and prices, it was revealed (on December 13, 1966) that Smith, Kline and French, a staunch P.M.A.C. member, sold 2.2 pounds of stelazine to druggists for about $57,000, aespite the fact that this amount can be imported into Canada, all taxes and duties paid, for as little as $200. I wanted to put that passage on the record, Mr. Speaker, to indicate to the house that we in this party are not blind to the fact that drug prices in this country are high, too high. Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-190 purports to have as its objective a beneficial effect on the cost of drugs for Canadians. We on this side of the house agree that any measure which will have the effect of lowering the price of drugs to the consumer, and prescription drugs especially, is advantageous to the people of this country, provided any saving in price is not outweighed by other resulting disadvantages.
Two years ago a special committee of the house was set up to consider this question and make recommendations respecting a comprehensive and effective program to reduce the price of drugs. The terms of reference under which the committee was established spoke only of the price of drugs. It seems so obvious that when we as Canadians speak of drugs we mean drugs that are of a high quality and will perform as effectively as possible the function which they are prescribed to perform. Therefore we assume that these are the kind of drugs the house had in mind when it referred this problem to the committee. The committee, in its report at page 6, chapter II entitled "Background to the Report", has this to say:
The committee's conclusions must be such that any of its recommendations, if adopted, should continue to maintain a proper balance between industry and consumer and take into consideration the importance of continued and increased scientific research in Canada. No recommendations could be considered, which, although designed to lower drug prices in Canada, might produce drugs of questionable safety or have a detrimental effect upon other aspects of the Canadian economy.
This is what the committee reasoned was its duty with regard to the responsibility placed upon it. We have heard unfortunately, a great deal of propaganda, I would say, to

They want to create this myth and then, like knights on white chargers, go charging against this fictitious myth, having the people believe that they are the sole protectors of the interests of the Canadian consumer.
The myth that the pharmaceutical industry of Canada is any worse than any other segment of our industry, or indeed any better than any other segment of our industry, has yet to be proven. I consider that the pharmaceutical industry of Canada has done a great deal for Canadians. We have benefited from their research. Any of us, if we think about it at all, will realize the tremendous benefits to mankind generally, and not only to Canadians, which have resulted from medical research in pharmaceuticals.
We think of the "wonder" drugs that have come into general use in the last few years, with their resulting beneficial reduction, and in some cases the wiping out, of diseases causing premature death and the elimination of prolonged illnesses because of treatment which may result in a rapid and complete recovery from many diseases which only a few years ago were often fatal.
Benefits resulting from these drugs far outweigh the total cost of all the drug research that has ever been carried out. It is true that some of these drugs have been discovered as the result of research in universities or in institutions supported by the taxpayers; but the industry, too, has made very worth-while contributions. We will always be indebted to the industry for the benefits to mankind which have resulted from this research. This type of research, of course, takes place in many parts of the world. All mankind benefits when some great, new breakthrough is made in pharmaceutical research.
Since all mankind benefits from these advances, it creates a very complicated problem as to how the discoverers of a new drug shall be adequately compensated for their contribution to mankind. The drug industry cannot be thought of as being in isolation in any one country, or indeed in any one group of countries, because when it produces a new advance in the treatment of disease our moral conscience requires that the new drug be available to everyone as quickly as possible.

Therefore, we have a very difficult problem in determining what is a reasonable benefit under the patent rights. Then too there is the question of proving that a new drug is a safe drug. There are many factors involved in the cost of drugs to the consumer. The members of the committee immediately recognized this. In addition to the cost of manufacturing there are many other factors. There is the cost of distribution, the professional cost of dispensing the drug, and the taxation involved at every stage in respect of the drug and the concerns which carry on the business of manufacturing, distributing or selling pharmaceuticals. All these factors, of course, are built into the cost of the drug, the same as in the case of other products. These costs have been increasing in recent years. This is part of the entire picture of the increased cost of living with which we are all so familiar. The federal government has jurisdiction with regard to some of these factors. Some of them, however, are under the control of other levels of government while others are under the control of the profession itself and are affected by other considerations.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman is paraphrasing what I actually said. The commitment that I gave in Winnipeg was that the Prime Minister's undertaking would be honoured. There has been no change in the government's position since that time. The Prime Minister undertook, as I understand, that the Air Canada base would remain open, or that an alternative solution would be found which would provide approximately equal employment opportunities in the aircraft maintenance industry. As my hon. friend undoubtedly is aware, we have made a special effort to try to reach a solution which will be satisfactory to everyone involved. A committee was formed with members of the provincial government and federal government, and they have been meeting and considering some of the suggestions which have been made. They are aware that there are at least several alternative possibilities, so far as the means which might be adopted to fulfil the commitment are concerned.
At the present time I cannot tell my hon. friend with certainty, though I should very much like to do so, which of the options that are being studied will be ultimately adopted. It is for this reason that the employees of Air Canada face a dilemma, the dilemma being whether to negotiate additional transfers under the contracts which now exist, and take advantage of the seniority rights which have been guaranteed, or whether to take their chances and remain at Winnipeg, in the hope that the ultimate solution will meet with their approval and provide satisfactory employment for them.
As I explained to the union officials, when I met them, I regret very much that this dilemma for the employees exists, but unfortunately I cannot do much about it right at this

moment. I hope that we shall be in a position to announce, in the not too distant future, what the ultimate solution will be. Unfortunately I am not in a position to do that now. Negotiations between the union and the company will be going on in the meantime. It is this aspect of the situation which is beyond my control. I wish it were within my control, but it is not and I am afraid that the union
